name: Connecting graphs to language and modern architectures
gist: Papers that bridge graph learning with large language models and transformers, enabling graphs to work with text and taking advantage of modern deep learning frameworks.
explain: For years, graph models and language models evolved separately. Language models use transformers—architecture where every word can attend to every other word, learning which parts matter most. Graph models use message-passing or spectral methods designed for network structure. But recently, researchers realized transformers can work on graphs too: you can treat nodes as tokens (a chunk of data the model reads) and let a transformer learn which connections matter. And you can combine graph and text data: some entities have names or descriptions, so you can use both graph structure and language at the same time.

The challenge is scaling and semantics. Transformers need to compute attention between every pair of nodes, which costs quadratic time and memory—impossible for graphs with millions of nodes. Also, transformers treat everything as sequence of tokens, so you need to encode graph structure into tokens somehow. And when graphs have varied metadata—text on nodes, multiple edge types—how do you represent that without drowning in complexity?

Papers propose several approaches: efficient transformers that approximate attention by sampling or using sparse patterns, so they scale to large graphs. They encode graph structure as special tokens or as positional encodings (information about where each node sits in the graph). They jointly learn from graph and text by feeding both into the same model—useful for knowledge graphs where entities have names, or for paper citations where papers have abstracts. Some adapt pretrained language models to graphs by treating neighborhoods as text or by treating edge sequences as pseudo-sentences. Others use language models as components in a larger graph system: asking the model to reason in natural language about what a neighborhood means, then using that reasoning to make decisions.

papers.title: Bridging Input Feature Spaces Towards Graph Foundation Models
papers.contribution: ALL-IN achieves strong performance on unseen datasets with new input features without architecture changes or retraining, enabling input-agnostic transferable graph models.

papers.title: Enhancing LLMs for Graph Tasks via Graph-aware LoRA Generation
papers.contribution: GaRA consistently outperforms baselines on zero-shot graph learning tasks by enabling LMs to leverage graph structure information through weight-level injection.

papers.title: Graph Tokenization for Bridging Graphs and Transformers
papers.contribution: Achieves state-of-the-art on 12 benchmarks, outperforming graph neural networks and specialized graph transformers without architectural modifications.

papers.title: Relational Graph Transformer
papers.contribution: Matches or outperforms GNN baselines by up to 18% across 21 RelBench tasks, establishing Graph Transformers for Relational Deep Learning.

papers.title: GFMate: Empowering Graph Foundation Models with Test-time Prompt Tuning
papers.contribution: Achieves improvements of up to 30.63% on 12 benchmark datasets by enabling test-time prompt tuning independent of source domain embedding and model pre-training strategy.

papers.title: Global-Recent Semantic Reasoning on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs with Large Language Models
papers.contribution: DyGRASP achieves up to 34% improvement in Hit@10 for destination node retrieval on dynamic graph benchmarks.

papers.title: HYPER: A Foundation Model for Inductive Link Prediction with Knowledge Hypergraphs
papers.contribution: Consistently outperforms existing methods in both node-only and node-and-relation inductive settings, showing strong generalization to unseen higher-arity relational structures.

papers.title: Modality-free Graph In-context Alignment
papers.contribution: Achieves superior few-shot performance across diverse graph domains and strong generalization to unseen domains without parameter updates.

papers.title: Platonic Transformers: A Solid Choice For Equivariance
papers.contribution: Achieves competitive performance on CIFAR-10, 3D point clouds, and molecular benchmarks while maintaining standard transformer efficiency.

papers.title: PromptDyG: Test-Time Prompt Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs
papers.contribution: PromptDyG theoretically guarantees larger similarity margin between positive and negative pairs, with consistent and significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on six benchmark datasets.
